summary: Rodent efficacy studies often report positive effects—62% of focal and 70% of global ischemia experiments were superior to control (O'Collins et al. 2006), and several clinical drug classes reproduced benefits in rodents (Sembach et al. 2021). However, translation is inconsistent: reported translation rates spanned 0–100% (Ritskes‑Hoitinga et al. 2022) and rodent→human concordance for liver effects was 44% (Leenaars et al. 2019).
why_range_is_wide: Range reflects heterogeneity across interventions, models, outcomes and likely selective reporting/publication bias noted by the authors.

summary: Mixed evidence: Spanagel 2017 reports three alcoholism drugs translated from rodent models (acamprosate, naltrexone, nalmefene) and consistent opioid-blockade effects in mice/rats; Pan et al. 2020 finds mouse tumor TGI does not predict approval (median 0.74 vs 0.77; AUC 0.45). Pan et al. cautions few approved drugs and TGI heterogeneity may limit inference.

summary: Rat efficacy findings are mixed: some rat-based results translated (three medications—acamprosate, naltrexone, nalmefene—and the incubation of drug‑seeking seen later in smokers, alcoholics, and cocaine addicts), but other rat‑effective agents failed clinically. Concordance depends on drug class and endpoint (e.g., 2 CRH‑R1 antagonists, KOR antagonists and buspirone failed; d‑amphetamine matched).
why_range_is_wide: Concordance varies by drug class and outcome (behavioral vs neurochemical): some neurochemical markers and certain medications translate, while several antagonist classes failed clinically.

summary: NHP drug-vs-food choice studies partially track human efficacy: d-amphetamine reduced cocaine choice in both humans and NHPs, but KOR antagonists and buspirone did not attenuate cocaine/methamphetamine/heroin choice. Females showed greater cocaine preference than males.
why_range_is_wide: Results differ by drug class, substance (stimulant vs opioid), and acute versus repeated dosing.

summary: No direct efficacy data; Leenaars et al. 2019 reports toxicity concordance instead, finding non‑rodent–human concordance for liver effects 40% (n=951). The study also reports 48% of adverse drug reactions were predictable from animal data (n=221) and notes predictivity higher for non‑rodents than rodents.

summary: Perel et al. 2007: in ewe models antenatal corticosteroids increased neonatal mortality (pooled OR 12.5, 95% CI 1.9–79.2), so sheep results did not match human trials (no benefit). The estimate is very imprecise (wide CI).
direction: evidence does not favour the model
why_range_is_wide: The wide confidence interval reflects imprecision from small numbers/few ewe studies.

summary: Evidence is mixed: dogs can predict or exclude some toxicities (LR+ 6.11 for cardiac disorders; 60% post-test odds for QT; Clark et al. 2018) but overall predictive power is modest—median PPV ≈0.67 and NPV ≈0.52 (Atkins et al. 2020). Absence of dog toxicity raised probability of no human toxicity to only ~72% (Bailey et al. 2019); species- and endpoint-specific differences reported (Jang et al. 2019).
why_range_is_wide: Performance varies by toxicity endpoint, severity and dataset (e.g., cardiac/QT vs subjective 'other' events; Liver‑Chip case studies vs regulatory databases).

why_range_is_wide: Performance varies by assay, endpoint and drug class (e.g., excluding β2‑agonists raised AUC from 0.81 to 0.91).

why_range_is_wide: Concordance varies by biological system and analysis type (whole transcriptome vs significant DEGs) and by specific disease model/diet (e.g., Western-diet vs choline-deficient).
